answer.sourceLine: This one is real and it is traceable to the sentence. It is Epistulae Morales ad Lucilium (Moral Letters to Lucilius), Letter 70, section 4 — in Latin, “Itaque sapiens vivet quantum debet, non quantum potest.” The familiar English is Richard M. Gummere’s Loeb Classical Library translation, whose Volume II appeared in 1920; his full sentence opens with “Accordingly,” which the circulating version simply trims.

source.heading: Letter 70, section 4

docMeta.dd: Epistulae Morales ad Lucilium, Letter 70 — “On the proper time to slip the cable”, section 4 (Book VIII of the letters)
c. AD 62–65, in the last years of Seneca’s life
“Itaque sapiens vivet quantum debet, non quantum potest.”
Richard M. Gummere, Loeb Classical Library, Volume II, 1920

source.excerpt: To such a life, as you are aware, one should not always cling. For mere living is not a good, but living well. Accordingly, the wise man will live as long as he ought, not as long as he can. He will mark in what place, with whom, and how he is to conduct his existence, and what he is about to do. He always reflects concerning the quality, and not the quantity, of his life.
trail: The Latin is in Book VIII of the letters: The Latin Library’s text of Epistula LXX ↗ reads, at section 4, “Itaque sapiens vivet quantum debet, non quantum potest.”

The English matches a printed edition word for word. Wikisource’s transcription ↗, made from the scan of Gummere’s Loeb Volume II, gives: “For mere living is not a good, but living well. Accordingly, the wise man will live as long as he ought, not as long as he can.”

The translation is dated by two independent records: the Internet Archive copy ↗ is catalogued as Volume 2, Heinemann, 1920, and the University of Utah’s Ethics of Suicide archive ↗ cites its Letter 70 text to Gummere, G. P. Putnam’s Sons, 1920, Vol. 2, pp. 57–73.

The Montaigne trail is real but downstream: Essays II.3 in Cotton’s translation ↗ contains “That the wise man lives as long as he ought, not so long as he can,” introduced as “the meaning of the sentence.”
source.excerptNote: Gummere’s 1920 English. The sentences immediately after this one make the letter’s real subject plain: Seneca is arguing that a wise man may end his own life once it can no longer be lived well.

source.rightsNote: Seneca’s Latin has been in the public domain for centuries. The English shown here is Richard M. Gummere’s Loeb Classical Library translation, whose Volume II was published in 1920 — well before 1931 — so that translation is also public domain in the United States. Note that this status attaches to Gummere’s wording specifically: a modern translation of the same Latin is a separate rights question.

author.name: Seneca the Younger
author.heading: Seneca the Younger
author.metaLine: c. 4 BC – AD 65 · Roman Stoic philosopher, dramatist & adviser to Nero
author.bio: Lucius Annaeus Seneca was a Roman Stoic philosopher, tragedian and statesman who served first as tutor and then as adviser to the emperor Nero. In his last years he withdrew from public life and wrote the Epistulae Morales ad Lucilium — 124 surviving letters of practical moral instruction composed roughly between spring 62 and spring 65 AD. In AD 65, caught in the aftermath of the Pisonian conspiracy, Nero ordered him to kill himself; he opened his veins and died slowly, still dictating to a scribe — which gives the line above a weight its usual inspirational framing never mentions.

misattribution.heading: What gets lost when it travels
misattribution.intro: The attribution to Seneca is correct — unusually so for a line this quotable. What goes wrong is everything around it: the translator disappears, the letter number disappears, the subject matter disappears, and a second author gets pulled in.

items.why: Montaigne’s essay “A Custom of the Island of Cea” (Essays II.3) ↗ carries the maxim in Charles Cotton’s English as “That the wise man lives as long as he ought, not so long as he can” — and Montaigne presents it as “the meaning of the sentence,” not as his own invention. Quote sites that lift it from there file it under his name; the sentence itself is Seneca’s.

Seneca wrote in Latin. This exact English is Gummere’s Loeb rendering, printed at Wikisource ↗ as “Accordingly, the wise man will live as long as he ought, not as long as he can.” The circulating version silently deletes the opening word and the translator.

Aggregators print the line with no work, no letter and no date — Goodreads ↗ gives the attribution as bare “— Seneca.” It is Letter 70, section 4, of the Moral Letters to Lucilius, and knowing that changes how the line reads, because Letter 70 is about choosing when to die.

misattribution.truthLine: Seneca really wrote it: “Itaque sapiens vivet quantum debet, non quantum potest” — Epistulae Morales 70.4 ↗. The English everyone quotes is Gummere’s, from the 1920 Loeb.

context.heading: Not a productivity slogan — a letter about choosing to die
lead: Letter 70 is not a meditation on making your days count. Its subject is voluntary death, and Gummere gave it the title “On the proper time to slip the cable.” Seneca builds the whole letter on a sailing image: life is a voyage, and the end of it is not a reef but the harbour every ship is bound for anyway. Some sailors are becalmed and worn down; others are carried home fast. Neither has grounds to complain.

The famous sentence is the hinge of that argument. Having said that “mere living is not a good, but living well,” Seneca concludes that a wise man measures his life by quality rather than by length — and that when the terms of it become intolerable, he may leave. Read on the page it comes from, the line is a Stoic defence of suicide as a rational option, not a line about seizing the day. Seneca died in AD 65 after Nero ordered him to take his own life.
context.detailsSummary: Whose English is this, and how Montaigne got dragged in
detailsBody: The wording everyone quotes is a translator’s. Richard Mott Gummere produced the Loeb Classical Library edition of the letters, and Letter 70 sits in Volume II, published in 1920. Because that edition is long out of copyright, its phrasing became the default English of Seneca online, and gets reprinted without Gummere’s name attached.

A second English route runs through Montaigne. His essay “A Custom of the Isle of Cea” (Essays, Book 2, Chapter 3) reaches the same conclusion and, in Charles Cotton’s translation, phrases it as “That the wise man lives as long as he ought, not so long as he can” — introduced there as the meaning of the sentence, not as something Montaigne is coining. That near-identical wording is why the line sometimes surfaces under Montaigne’s name.

sourcesVerified.claim: Wikisource's transcription of Moral Letters to Lucilius, Letter 70 (trans. Richard Mott Gummere) contains, in section 4, 'For mere living is not a good, but living well. Accordingly, the wise man will live as long as he ought, not as long as he can.' followed in section 5 by 'He always reflects concerning the quality, and not the quantity, of his life.'

The Latin Library's text of Seneca, Epistulae Morales Liber VIII contains at Epistula LXX section 4: 'Itaque sapiens vivet quantum debet, non quantum potest. [5] Videbit ubi victurus sit, cum quibus, quomodo, quid acturus.'

Wikiquote's Seneca the Younger page lists 'The wise man will live as long as he ought, not as long as he can' in its Epistulae Morales ad Lucilium section under Letter LXX, line 4, crediting the translation to Richard Mott Gummere.
The Internet Archive item 'Seneca Ad Lucilium Epistulae Morales VOLUME 2 (of 3), Gummere' is catalogued with publication date 1920 and publisher Heinemann.

The University of Utah's Ethics of Suicide Digital Archive reproduces Seneca's Letter 70 including 'the wise man will live as long as he ought, not as long as he can', and cites its text to Seneca, Ad Lucilium Epistulae Morales, Letters 70, 77, 78, trans. Richard M. Gummere, New York: G. P. Putnam's Sons, 1920, Vol. 2, pp. 57-73, 169-199.

HyperEssays' edition of Montaigne's Essays Book 2, Chapter 3, 'A Custom of the Island of Cea' (translated by Charles Cotton, 1685, revised by W. Carew Hazlitt, 1877) contains: 'This is the meaning of the sentence, "That the wise man lives as long as he ought, not so long as he can'.
Monadnock's text of Montaigne's 'A Custom of the Isle of Cea', translated by Charles Cotton, likewise contains 'That the wise man lives as long as he ought, not so long as he can'.
Goodreads displays the quote 'The wise man will live as long as he ought, not as long as he can' with the attribution line reading only '- Seneca', giving no book, letter number or translator.

Wikipedia gives Seneca the Younger's dates as c. 4 BC - AD 65, describes him as tutor and then adviser to Nero, and states that in AD 65, in the aftermath of the Pisonian conspiracy, 'Nero ordered him to kill himself'; he opened his veins and died slowly.
Wikipedia states the Epistulae Morales ad Lucilium comprise 124 extant letters written in the last years of Seneca's life, spanning roughly spring 62 AD to his death in spring 65 AD.
